## THE CURRENT MAP
31:27/q01 What does law imply in this supposition? [وَلَوْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether an unreal condition entails that the consequent fails without it.)
  31:27/q01/p1 It links an immense hypothetical to non-exhaustion without implying exhaustion otherwise. — reasons: Sībawayh, Ibn Mālik, Burhān and Ibn ʿĀshūr separate the conditional link from independent truth; Burhān says fewer supplies strengthen the denial. Al-Samīn rejects the simple counterfactual slogan.
  31:27/q01/p2 It only joins past condition and result without asserting either's failure. — reasons: Al-Itqān reports this first view and Ibn Hishām's objection; al-Zamakhsharī links verbal propositions.
  31:27/q01/p3 It conventionally negates the result when its condition fails. — reasons: Al-Itqān reports the widespread account but notes this verse as a difficulty; Burhān tests it against Suhayb's obedience and 8:23.
31:27/q02 How does annamā function after law? [أَنَّمَا · grammar] (turns on: Whether law licenses a nominal predicate and whether an existential predicate is supplied.)
  31:27/q02/p1 The anna clause has mā as noun and aqlām as nominal predicate. — reasons: Sībawayh says annamā can stand where anna can, unlike independent innamā; al-Mubarrad makes the clause a subject of implied existence, while others move an omitted predicate before or after. Al-Ṣaffār and poems support the construction.
  31:27/q02/p2 A nominal predicate after law anna is valid and refutes a strict verbal requirement. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn cite common Arabic and poems; Ibn al-Ḥājib concurs.
  31:27/q02/p3 A verbal predicate is required only with a derived predicate; aqlām is outside that rule. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī narrows al-Zamakhsharī's rule and excludes a wish construction at 33:20.
  31:27/q02/p4 The noun after law is subject to an omitted existential verb. — reasons: Burhān reports the Kufan estimate 'if it were established that.'
31:27/q03 What does min shajaratin specify? [مِن شَجَرَةٍ · grammar] (turns on: Whether specification attaches to mā or its locative pronoun.)
  31:27/q03/p1 It specifies mā or its locative pronoun and encompasses the whole class of earthly trees. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give these grammatical analyses; al-Ālūsī compares an indefinite in a conditional and Ibn ʿAbbās's date-and-locust analogy.
31:27/q04 Why is shajarah singular? [مِن شَجَرَةٍ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the singular distributes each tree or names the whole class.)
  31:27/q04/p1 It distributes the picture tree by tree until none is omitted. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Rāzī, Biqāʿī and Bursevī stress exhaustive individual treatment.
  31:27/q04/p2 It denotes the class; each tree can yield many pens from its branches. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān cites indefinite singular parallels at 2:106 and 35:2; al-Ālūsī objects that a lone singular does not formally mean 'tree by tree' and one pen per tree would weaken the image; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes suitable branches.
31:27/q05 What is aqlām? [أَقْلَٰمٌۭ · meaning]
  31:27/q05/p1 Pens are cut and sharpened writing tools, potentially many from each tree. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī describes trimmed branches; Bursevī derives qalam from cutting and distinguishes kinds of cutting; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes a split reed. Al-Ālūsī calls aqlām formally a paucity plural because qilām is rare.
  31:27/q05/p2 No parallel supply of pens is needed, because one pen writes many books. — reasons: Al-Rāzī contrasts quickly consumed ink with a pen's long use; al-Biqāʿī infers omitted ink and more trees.
31:27/q06 Which sea is intended? [وَٱلْبَحْرُ · referent] (turns on: Whether the article points to the known ocean, all seas, or fresh water.)
  31:27/q06/p1 The sea generically, including Earth's seas. — reasons: Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī make the first sea generic; al-Ṭībī takes its article as replacing Earth's possessive pronoun.
  31:27/q06/p2 The great encircling ocean. — reasons: Bursevī describes its inlets, depth, islands, jinn cities and Iblīs's throne; al-Ālūsī prefers the known greatest sea.
  31:27/q06/p3 Fresh water that grows trees for pens. — reasons: Abū ʿUbaydah argues salt water cannot grow the pens; Majāz notes inland country may also be called a sea.
  31:27/q06/p4 Bahr lexically denotes broad or abundant water and can have figurative uses. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī cites a broad-striding horse, a prophetic use for abundance, briny water poetry, bāḥir for a fool and baḥrah for a locality.
31:27/q07 How is al-baḥr read? [وَٱلْبَحْرُ · readings] (turns on: Which transmitted case or wording is followed.)
  31:27/q07/p1 Accusative al-baḥra, attributed chiefly to Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb. — reasons: Ibn Mujāhid says Abū ʿAmr alone in his list; al-Nashr names two Basrans, while other accounts add Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both cases.
  31:27/q07/p2 Nominative al-baḥru, the majority reading. — reasons: Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī name the majority; Ibn ʿUmar reports prophetic nominative recitation. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both cases.
  31:27/q07/p3 Indefinite nominative wa-baḥrun is read by Ibn Masʿūd and Ṭalḥah. — reasons: Ibn Jinnī supplies 'there is a sea'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn allow a circumstantial wāw; al-Ālūsī prefers the stated verb as predicate.
  31:27/q07/p4 Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad reads 'the sea is its ink' (madāduhu). — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls madād a verbal noun; al-Ṭabrisī rejects taking seawater merely as addition to other ink.
31:27/q08 How is the sea clause parsed? [وَٱلْبَحْرُ يَمُدُّهُۥ · grammar] (turns on: Whether it is circumstantial or coordinated within the law clause.)
  31:27/q08/p1 It is a new circumstantial nominal clause with al-baḥr as subject and yamudduhu as predicate. — reasons: Sībawayh estimates 'the sea is in this state'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī prefer wāw al-ḥāl, with no linking pronoun required. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it supplies the simultaneous ink state.
  31:27/q08/p2 Accusative al-baḥr coordinates with mā, the noun of anna. — reasons: Sībawayh gives the verse as an example. Ibn al-Ḥājib says yamudduhu must predicate the sea if no other predicate is given; al-Ṭabrisī prefers elided 'ink' as predicate and makes the verb circumstantial.
  31:27/q08/p3 Nominative al-baḥr coordinates with the syntactic position or sense of anna. — reasons: Ibn Jinnī cites 9:3; al-Zamakhsharī permits it. Abū Ḥayyān says it depends on a disputed subject parse after law, while al-Ālūsī questions crossing an omitted predicate.
  31:27/q08/p4 Accusative al-baḥr depends on an omitted verb explained by yamudduhu. — reasons: Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn and Qiraat-ER report this; al-Ālūsī also mentions an omitted thābit.
  31:27/q08/p5 The sea clause implicitly means 'earth's sea' to provide a possessive link. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī proposes this; Abū Ḥayyān objects that the nominal circumstantial clause needs no such link and the article-for-pronoun parse is Kufan.
31:27/q09 How is yamudduhu read? [يَمُدُّهُۥ · readings] (turns on: Whether the verb is from madda or amadda and whether the subject is treated as feminine.)
  31:27/q09/p1 Some read the causative form from amadda with ḍamma on the yāʾ. — reasons: Attributed variously to al-Aʿraj, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Ibn Muṣarrif and Ibn Masʿūd; Ibn Jinnī compares army reinforcements and rivers, citing 8:9. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it loses the inkwell nuance.
  31:27/q09/p2 Some read feminine tamudduhu. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās or Ubayy are named; the seven seas are construed as feminine subject.
  31:27/q09/p3 The majority reads masculine yamudduhu from madda. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls it the common reading; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies its vowels.
31:27/q10 What does yamudduhu mean here? [يَمُدُّهُۥ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the verb evokes ink supply or a general extension.)
  31:27/q10/p1 Seven seas continually replenish the first as ink replenishes an inkpot. — reasons: Al-Yazīdī compares adding water to a pot; al-Zamakhsharī, Nasafī and al-Ālūsī use an inkwell image; al-Ālūsī notes the imperfect form, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says ink is implicit.
  31:27/q10/p2 Madda extends or adds gradually, while amadda denotes external assistance or supply. — reasons: Al-Māwardī, Abū Zayd, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Qurṭubī report distinctions, comparing rivers, wells, money and troops; Ibn Qutaybah connects this use to midād ink.
  31:27/q10/p3 Madda and amadda can be synonymous dialect variants. — reasons: Groups reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn al-Shaykh, see no material difference.
31:27/q11 What does the pronoun in yamudduhu refer to? [يَمُدُّهُۥ · referent]
  31:27/q11/p1 The first sea. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭabrisī make the antecedent explicit.
31:27/q12 What does min baʿdihi mean? [مِنۢ بَعْدِهِۦ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the relation is spatial/additive or temporal.)
  31:27/q12/p1 From behind or in addition to the first sea. — reasons: Majāz pictures seven seas flowing into the first; al-Baghawī says behind and additional; al-Ālūsī allows this.
  31:27/q12/p2 After the first sea's ink has been used up. — reasons: Al-Ālūsī presents this as an alternative.
31:27/q13 What are the seven added seas? [سَبْعَةُ أَبْحُرٍۢ · referent] (turns on: Whether they are imagined equivalents or particular physical waters.)
  31:27/q13/p1 Actual seas or rivers identified in reports. — reasons: Ibn ʿAmr reports alternating seven fire and water seas below the sea; Bursevī cites China, Tibet, India, Sind, Persia, East and West, and separately suggests seven named rivers; al-Irshād speaks of mountain-fed waterways. No grading is stated.
  31:27/q13/p2 Imagined seas comparable to the first. — reasons: Al-Rāzī places them beyond existing seas; al-Ālūsī makes each match the ocean in extent and water; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī agrees.
  31:27/q13/p3 A literal seven seas surrounding the world is unconfirmed Israelite material. — reasons: Ibn Kathīr rejects deriving a fixed cosmography from the number.
31:27/q14 Why say seven 
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<31:27 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
and abḥur? [سَبْعَةُ أَبْحُرٍۢ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether seven is a limit or a sign of abundance.)
  31:27/q14/p1 Seven means great abundance and does not limit further supply. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says even a thousand would not change the point; Ibn Kathīr invokes 18:109's repeated supply. Al-Ālūsī cites heavens, planets, regions and days and the believer-one/unbeliever-seven saying; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it idiomatic.
  31:27/q14/p2 Abḥur is a paucity plural suited to the numeral seven. — reasons: Burhān, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī note grammatical matching even where the image indicates abundance.
  31:27/q14/p3 Seven is a customary complete count with symbolic extensions. — reasons: Al-Rāzī derives it from seven climes, days and planets, three as minimal completeness and seven as the larger part of ten; he compares ritual threes, Hell's seven gates, Paradise's eight and al-Farrāʾ's 'wāw of eight.'
31:27/q15 What action is left implicit? [أَقْلَٰمٌۭ وَٱلْبَحْرُ كَلِمَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ · rhetoric]
  31:27/q15/p1 The pens and seas write God's words as ink and writing materials, then run out first. — reasons: Abū ʿUbaydah calls it compressed; al-Ṭabarī says pens break and ink dries. Al-Fārisī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī compare other omitted actions at 26:63, 2:196 and 27:28–29; al-Biqāʿī and Islahi note omitted ink.
31:27/q16 What is the response to law? [مَّا نَفِدَتْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether mā naf idat is itself the answer.)
  31:27/q16/p1 Mā naf idat is the expressed answer. — reasons: Burhān says denial amid great supply proves denial with less; al-Ālūsī calls it the jawāb.
  31:27/q16/p2 The answer about exhausted materials is omitted before the stated denial. — reasons: Burhān offers this as an alternative, with possible omitted conjunction.
31:27/q17 What does naf idat mean? [مَّا نَفِدَتْ · meaning]
  31:27/q17/p1 To reach an end through exhaustion over time. — reasons: Al-Māwardī contrasts it with perishing all at once; al-Zajjāj applies the denial to God's words.
31:27/q18 What are God's kalimāt? [كَلِمَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ · referent] (turns on: Whether the term refers to knowledge, creative acts, eternal speech, revelation or promises.)
  31:27/q18/p1 God's decrees, possible creations, signs and wonders brought about by Be. — reasons: Al-Rāzī argues cause-for-effect naming and cites Jesus as a word; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 36:82 and 4:171; Islahi says signs manifest the creative command. Al-Ālūsī's Imam prefers this connection to 31:26.
  31:27/q18/p2 God's limitless knowledge, known realities and wisdom. — reasons: Muqātil and al-Suddī include wonders; al-Naḥḥās details kinds, parts, qualities and change; al-Wāḥidī reasons limitless knowledge entails limitless expressing words. Abū ʿAlī distinguishes still-possible things from those already existing.
  31:27/q18/p3 God's eternal speech and meanings, including utterances, revelation and creative commands. — reasons: Al-Qushayrī contrasts finite writers with eternal word; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes speech to angels and prophets and the command Be. Al-Rāzī distinguishes created letters and arrangement from divine attributes.
  31:27/q18/p4 God's favors for the obedient, or promised reward and threatened punishment. — reasons: Al-Māwardī reports Paradise favors; Abū Muslim extends this to unseen reward and punishment.
  31:27/q18/p5 The Qur'an and further revelation to Muhammad. — reasons: Qatādah's reported occasion answers a prediction that recitation will soon end; Ibn ʿĀshūr says this reading implies much more revelation.
  31:27/q18/p6 Kalimāt has other Quranic senses outside this verse. — reasons: Al-Dāmghānī lists rites, Adam's received words, tawḥīd, creative wonders, Jesus, religion and the Quran.
31:27/q19 Why use the plural kalimāt? [كَلِمَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the small plural has force here.)
  31:27/q19/p1 Even a small number of God's words exceeds these supplies, all the more His total speech. — reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī make the a fortiori claim; al-Samīn invokes Ḥassān's jufanāt.
  31:27/q19/p2 A sound plural in a general construction need not mean a small number. — reasons: Al-Shaykh objects to the strict paucity reading; al-Samīn notes debate about whether the article marks generality.
31:27/q20 What does the image establish? [* · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the comparison asserts a precise quantity or simply proves inexhaustibility.)
  31:27/q20/p1 Finite materials, pages, writers and lives cannot exhaust divine words, knowledge, decrees or signs. — reasons: Muqātil says all creation's pens would fail; al-Ḥasan says the writer dies; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says adding more cannot establish a limit. Burhān says non-exhaustion holds before and after ink is spent; Islahi says science has only found a drop.
  31:27/q20/p2 The wording denies exhaustion without asserting a precise limit on the imagined materials. — reasons: Burhān reports careful scholars using al-Khiḍr's bird-and-sea analogy; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also rejects a bound beyond the stated seas.
31:27/q21 What follows about divine speech? [كَلِمَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ · theology] (turns on: Whether kalimāt must denote eternal speech or can denote limitless referents.)
  31:27/q21/p1 God's speech is eternal and uncreated, so its meanings do not end. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī infers uncreatedness; al-Qurṭubī prefers eternal speech on contextual grounds; Bursevī infers Quranic pre-eternity; al-Rāzī distinguishes divine attribute from created letters.
  31:27/q21/p2 Limitless knowledge and possibilities can be called words without treating them as eternal speech. — reasons: Abū ʿAlī confines some referents to future possibilities; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah observes this tends toward Muʿtazilī created-speech doctrine; al-Fārisī reports a wisdom-and-workmanship reading.
31:27/q22 What do Mighty and Wise contribute? [عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌۭ · interpretation]
  31:27/q22/p1 God cannot be thwarted and nothing escapes His knowledge and wise governance, so His words do not end. — reasons: Muqātil says mighty in kingdom and wise in command; Ibn Kathīr extends wisdom through creation, law and speech. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the closure against hopes of prophetic failure; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links it to God's sole governance; Islahi links unity, prophethood and resurrection.
31:27/q23 What occasion is reported? [* · reports] (turns on: Who challenged the message and on what issue.)
  31:27/q23/p1 Jewish scholars challenged little human knowledge by citing the Torah and great wisdom. — reasons: Versions place direct inquiry in Medina or through Quraysh in Mecca, sometimes starting with the spirit at 17:85 or wisdom at 2:269. One names Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab; another brings Torah stoning and 5:43. The Prophet says Torah knowledge is much for people yet little beside God's. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah prefers this occasion.
  31:27/q23/p2 Polytheists or Quraysh predicted Muhammad's speech would end. — reasons: Qatādah and others give this report; al-Suddī varies it to a complaint that Muhammad spoke abundantly. Al-Ālūsī calls its contextual connection weak.
  31:27/q23/p3 Some Jews predicted the recited words themselves would cease. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports this distinct Jewish version.
31:27/q24 Where was the verse revealed? [* · sciences] (turns on: Whether the Jewish exchange happened after migration or through Meccan intermediaries.)
  31:27/q24/p1 In Medina, as an exception to the Meccan sūra. — reasons: ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās are cited; reports vary between two and three exceptional verses beginning here. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah prefers Medina. Ibn ʿĀshūr says prophetic direction then fixed its place.
  31:27/q24/p2 In Mecca, whether as part of the sūra or after Jews instructed Quraysh. — reasons: Ibn Kathīr prefers the familiar Meccan classification despite Medinan reports; Ibn ʿĀshūr says a Meccan account fits its revealed sequence.
31:27/q25 How does it connect to the sūra? [* · links] (turns on: Which surrounding argument it advances.)
  31:27/q25/p1 It extends claims of divine ownership, knowledge and sole governance to limitless dominion and creative commands. — reasons: Al-Rāzī says 31:26 could seem finite; Ibn ʿĀshūr links hidden knowledge at 31:16 and 31:23; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links exclusive governance; Biqāʿī connects resurrection wisdom.
  31:27/q25/p2 It supports the sūra's argument for revelation against Quranic opponents. — reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites the sūra's opening and 31:6–7; Ibn ʿĀshūr follows the theme to 31:34; Islahi says abundant signs answer demands for more.
  31:27/q25/p3 It offers signs of power and unity against polytheism. — reasons: Al-Qaffāl and al-Qurṭubī read the wonders as proofs; Islahi says their abundance leaves no excuse for idol worship.
31:27/q26 How does it relate to 18:109? [* · links]
  31:27/q26/p1 The sea-as-ink image there likewise states inexhaustibility. — reasons: Many commentators cite 18:109; Ibn Kathīr reads its 'another like it' as unlimited repeated supply. Ibn ʿĀshūr links Luqmān with Cave and Dhū l-Qarnayn narratives, and distinguishes completion of words in 6:115 as fulfillment.
31:27/q27 How much is human knowledge beside God's? [* · interpretation]
  31:27/q27/p1 Much by a human measure, yet little beside God's knowledge. — reasons: ʿIkrimah says Torah wisdom suffices for salvation; al-Rabīʿ compares human knowledge to a drop beside seas. Ibn ʿĀshūr says God wisely discloses some knowledge and withholds other knowledge.
31:27/q28 What inward lesson is drawn? [* · inward]
  31:27/q28/p1 Wisdom can flow without end from God's inexhaustible treasury. — reasons: Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz describes sages' speech; Bursevī adds knowers receiving insight in a flash and finite pages unable to contain eternal meanings.
  31:27/q28/p2 God's pre-eternal words invite the servant to love and felicity. — reasons: Al-Junayd links continuous blessings with love, divine choosing and future felicity.
31:27/q29 What broader examples illustrate inexhaustibility? [* · interpretation]
  31:27
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<31:27 update 1, part 2 of 0..2>>
/q29/p1 Natural research, medicine, mercy and the afterlife far exceed human inquiry. — reasons: Al-Rāzī surveys bodies, minerals, plants, animals, illnesses and medicines; reports two ungraded Galen dream narratives; compares human time to God's domain and urges lasting deeds.
  31:27/q29/p2 Worldly power passes and invites ascetic detachment. — reasons: Bursevī quotes ʿAṭṭār on death and Ibrāhīm ibn Adham.
31:27/q30 How is the verse used in discussion of Quranic inimitability? [* · rhetoric]
  31:27/q30/p1 Its composition and meanings exceed human learned rhetorical craft. — reasons: Al-Bāqillānī contrasts teachable meter and badīʿ with consistent Quranic excellence; Burhān says varied retellings avoid tedium, with addition, omission and rearrangement; al-Rāghib says a short Quran holds uncountable meaning.
  31:27/q30/p2 Its rhetoric calls for whole-Quran comparison of words, style and context. — reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ describes her lexical and comparative method, influence of her father and al-Khūlī, and the Arab eloquence miracle alongside Moses' and Jesus' signs.
  31:27/q30/p3 The seven Ḥawāmīm emphasize revelation from the Mighty, Wise God. — reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes their consecutive revelation and canonical order, Ḥā Mīm openings, al-Shūrā's added letters and Arabic revelation formula.
31:27/q31 What ancillary comparisons do commentators make? [* · links]
  31:27/q31/p1 Lexical and poetic comparisons illuminate broad Arabic usage. — reasons: Ibn Jinnī cites dialectal ṣād/sīn/zāy variation; al-Jurjānī discusses Abū Tammām's metaphor of poetic ideas and word craft; Burhān reports a variant of Jarīr's line.
  31:27/q31/p2 Adjacent discussions address resurrection and cross-reference other sūras. — reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports a question about gradual growth and sudden resurrection; Ibn al-Jawzī cross-refers Hūd, al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Baqarah.
  31:27/q31/p3 Innamā is a non-governing restrictive construction unlike dependent annamā. — reasons: Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh cite independent-clause examples; al-Jurjānī reports mā ... illā analyses and warns the two constructions are not interchangeable.

## THE NEW NOTES
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p100/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The universe contains such abundant signs of God’s power and wisdom that even all trees as pens and all seas plus seven more as ink could not record them.

<<end of input>>

item.text: The note treats God’s words as signs throughout the universe and uses the pens and seas image to show that those signs cannot be fully recorded. I’ll add it to the existing positions for those two points.
